paragraphs: Identifying a dynamical system means recovering its governing parameters from an observed trajectory. Scientific systems often have symmetries: transformations of the system’s state that interact predictably with its evolution. This paper asks how much those symmetries can reduce the amount of trajectory data needed, including when the symmetry group is initially unknown.

The authors first analyze the case where the symmetry is supplied. They show that identification can require a significantly shorter single trajectory than in the generic setting and precisely characterize that improvement. They then develop a method that learns the symmetry group from the trajectory and incorporates the discovered structure into parameter identification.

In the analyzed setting, discovering the symmetry achieves the same optimal trajectory length as knowing it beforehand. This makes symmetry discovery part of the statistical efficiency result, rather than merely an additional descriptive output. The analysis combines group representation theory with expansion properties of Cayley graphs to explain how structural constraints enable identification from less observation.
icml-2026-adaptive-symmetry-discovery-fo.tldr: The proposed method discovers a dynamical system’s symmetry from one trajectory and matches the optimal trajectory length available when that symmetry is known.

paragraphs: A language model can handle many unfamiliar prompts yet become unreliable when inputs depart from its training distribution. This paper studies that boundary through the model’s internal computations. Its mechanistic framework asks whether changes in the concepts used during processing can reveal distribution shifts that are difficult to characterize from the prompt alone.

In systematic experiments, the authors find that out-of-distribution inputs, including subtle typing errors and jailbreak prompts, lead models to operate on more internally represented concepts that the authors characterize as fallacious. These observations provide a signal for estimating how far a prompt departs from familiar conditions and for examining what happens inside the model during that departure.

The authors use this signal to motivate a fine-tuning strategy aimed at improving robustness. The contribution also broadens the diagnostic question: an input may be concerning because of the computational behavior it induces, not just its visible wording. The reported findings support internal monitoring as a way to study robustness and guide adaptation, without establishing universal protection against unfamiliar inputs.
icml-2026-at-the-edge-of-understanding-s.tldr: Internal concept activity provides a signal of distribution shift in language models and guides a fine-tuning strategy for improving robustness.

paragraphs: UniDFlow brings multimodal understanding, generation, and editing into one discrete flow-matching framework. Combining these abilities creates a training challenge because the demands of interpreting content and producing content can interfere. The proposed design gives the tasks distinct adaptation components while keeping them within a unified model.

Specifically, task-specific low-rank adapters separate understanding from generation to avoid interference between objectives and entanglement of their representations. A reference-based preference alignment procedure then compares relative outcomes under the same conditioning. Holding that conditioning fixed focuses alignment on differences between the outputs, improving faithfulness and controllability without requiring large-scale retraining.

The authors report state-of-the-art results across eight benchmarks and strong generalization to tasks without explicit task-specific training. Those tasks include filling missing image regions, generating images from contextual examples, editing with a reference, and composing requested content. Together, the findings indicate that separating task adaptation and aligning relative outcomes can support several multimodal capabilities within the same framework, including capabilities beyond its explicitly trained tasks.
icml-2026-best-of-both-worlds-multimodal.tldr: UniDFlow combines multimodal understanding, generation, and editing through separate task adapters and reference-based preference alignment, with strong reported benchmark and zero-shot results.

paragraphs: Models of physical dynamics often need to respect how their inputs and outputs transform under a system’s symmetries. Clifford-Steerable CNNs build such relationships into their architecture. This paper identifies a restriction in their standard formulation: the available kernel basis is incomplete, which limits the transformations the model can represent even while respecting its required symmetries.

The proposed Conditional Clifford-Steerable CNNs expand the kernels using equivariant representations of the input feature field. Consequently, the kernels can depend on the current input while retaining the prescribed transformation behavior. The authors derive the constraint that these input-dependent kernels must satisfy and show how an implicit parameterization solves it efficiently.

The framework accommodates arbitrary pseudo-Euclidean symmetry groups and is tested on several partial differential equation forecasting tasks, including fluid dynamics and relativistic electrodynamics. It consistently improves on standard Clifford-Steerable CNNs in these experiments and performs comparably to state-of-the-art baselines. The results support input conditioning as a way to increase expressive capacity without discarding the physical symmetry structure built into the model.
icml-2026-conditional-clifford-steerable.tldr: Input-dependent equivariant kernels expand Clifford-Steerable CNN capacity and improve their reported performance on physical-system forecasting tasks.

paragraphs: Conditional kernel ridge regression allows a selected class of features to enter a regression model without being penalized. It can be understood as fitting those features through linear regression and then using ordinary kernel ridge regression to explain the remaining target variation. This paper studies when that separation improves prediction and how to analyze its statistical behavior.

The main result relates conditional regression to ordinary kernel ridge regression with a fixed residual kernel. The reduction introduces an additional expected test-risk term bounded at order one over the square root of the sample size. Its hidden constant depends on the selected function class and the input distribution, so the comparison retains those dependencies.

The authors apply this analysis to features given by leading kernel eigenfunctions and to features sampled from a random-feature representation. They establish a close relationship between these settings. Theory and experiments show improvements over standard kernel ridge regression when the target’s component in the unpenalized feature class is more pronounced than its residual component.
icml-2026-conditional-krr-injecting-unpe.tldr: Conditional kernel ridge regression can improve prediction when selected unpenalized features capture a stronger target component than the remaining residual.

paragraphs: Strong benchmark performance does not necessarily establish that an image model has learned meaningful biological concepts. This paper investigates that distinction in cell culture and tissue microscopy, two widely available imaging settings at different biological scales. The central question is whether existing representation-learning methods consistently capture high-level biological information.

The authors compare current methods with deliberately simple baselines on curated benchmarks. These include models that have not been trained and representations describing cellular tissue structure. Across a considerable subset of evaluation settings, these baselines perform comparably to state-of-the-art methods. That result challenges what the corresponding benchmark scores can establish about the quality of learned representations.

The finding does not imply that every microscopy model fails to learn useful biology. It shows that many commonly used evaluation metrics can conceal the absence of relevant high-level abstractions. Detailed comparisons with simple baselines also help interpret individual models’ strengths and weaknesses. The study therefore argues for improving both learning methods and benchmarks so that reported progress better reflects what models actually learn.
icml-2026-deep-learning-for-bioimaging-w.tldr: Simple and untrained baselines rival advanced microscopy models in many evaluated settings, exposing weaknesses in how biological representation quality is measured.

paragraphs: A function can be complicated when viewed directly from its inputs yet become simpler when expressed as a sequence of intermediate computations. This paper uses that compositional structure to study why an additional network layer can provide a real learning advantage. The analysis takes place in a controlled setting with high-dimensional Gaussian inputs.

The authors examine an explicit three-layer fitting model trained through spectral estimators applied layer by layer. Although the overall target is a high-degree polynomial, the intermediate representation exposes structure unavailable at the input level. Learning can therefore proceed through simpler spectral estimation problems, whereas a shallow estimator must resolve the components together.

Using Gaussian universality, the analysis establishes sharp differences in sample complexity between the two-layer and three-layer strategies. The result gives a concrete mechanism connecting depth to data requirements: intermediate representations change which structure becomes accessible at each stage. Its theoretical force comes from the specified compositional targets and Gaussian setting, rather than from a claim that adding depth improves every learning problem.
icml-2026-deep-learning-of-compositional.tldr: For compositional targets under Gaussian inputs, layer-wise spectral learning reveals structure that yields sharp sample-complexity advantages for three layers over two.

paragraphs: In decentralized stochastic gradient descent, multiple participants train while exchanging information through a communication network. Earlier theory suggested that poorly connected networks, characterized by a small spectral gap, substantially slow convergence both when participants’ data are homogeneous and when they are heterogeneous. Experiments have often shown a weaker topology effect in the homogeneous case.

This paper develops a tighter convergence analysis to address that mismatch. Instead of summarizing the network through its spectral gap alone, the new analysis accounts for every eigenvalue of the mixing matrix that describes information exchange. This provides a more detailed mathematical description of how the communication structure affects the optimization process.

The authors carefully evaluate convergence experimentally and report that their analysis describes topology effects more accurately than prior bounds. The contribution is a refined account of an existing algorithm, helping explain why changing network connectivity can have different consequences across data settings. It also shows why one summary statistic of a communication network may miss behavior relevant to practical training.
icml-2026-improved-convergence-analysis-.tldr: A convergence analysis using the mixing matrix’s full spectrum better explains how communication topology affects decentralized SGD.

paragraphs: Confined acoustic spaces can affect different sound frequencies very differently, especially when resonance and reverberation are strong. INFER models those effects directly through a continuous, complex-valued frequency response field. This places frequency-dependent behavior at the center of learning, addressing difficulties encountered by acoustic fields based on time-domain impulse responses.

The framework jointly learns how attenuation and phase delay vary with frequency and position in three-dimensional space. A physics-based Kramers–Kronig consistency constraint links those quantities to regularize the model according to causality. Its spectral supervision also accounts for perception and hardware, placing emphasis on auditory bands identified as especially important.

The authors evaluate INFER on room-scale benchmarks and highly reverberant environments, including real car cabins. They report reductions of over 39% in average magnitude reconstruction error and over 51% in average phase reconstruction error against time-domain and hybrid-domain baselines. These findings support direct frequency-response learning as an effective approach for representing the frequency-selective behavior of the evaluated acoustic environments.
icml-2026-infer-learning-implicit-neural.tldr: INFER directly learns spatial frequency responses with physical consistency constraints, substantially improving reported acoustic magnitude and phase reconstruction.

paragraphs: Different human preferences can demand conflicting behavior from the same language model. Inference-time alignment offers flexibility by adapting a model’s outputs to different criteria when it is used. That flexibility can be computationally expensive, however, because alignment procedures often require multiple forward passes through the base model for each response.

Inference-aware meta-alignment changes how the base model is trained. The aim is to prepare a model that different inference-time alignment algorithms can efficiently move toward multiple task optima. This makes the later alignment procedure part of the training objective and seeks to retain preference flexibility with minimal additional computation during use.

The resulting training problems are nonlinear, motivating the proposed non-linear GRPO algorithm. The authors prove convergence to the optimal solution in the space of probability measures. That mathematical setting specifies the scope of the convergence claim; it is not a blanket guarantee about every neural-network implementation. The contribution connects preparation during training with efficient adaptation to diverse criteria at inference time.
icml-2026-inference-aware-meta-alignment.tldr: IAMA trains language models for efficient inference-time alignment and introduces non-linear GRPO with an optimality guarantee in probability-measure space.

paragraphs: Anytime-valid statistical tests allow evidence to be checked as observations arrive, but a strict deadline changes which evidence-gathering strategy is useful. This paper studies tests and confidence sequences for bounded means when no more than N observations are available. It frames the choice of statistical bets as a finite-horizon control problem.

The state records elapsed time and the logarithm of the test’s accumulated wealth. In certain interior regions, the authors prove that substantial deviations from Kelly betting are suboptimal and that Kelly betting reaches the decision threshold with high probability. Elsewhere, sufficient conditions favor more aggressive bets when behind schedule and less aggressive bets when ahead.

These conditional results motivate a phase diagram rather than a universally best betting rule. Guided by it, the authors train one Deep Q-Network policy using synthetic experience. The policy maps simple summaries of past observations to bets across different deadlines and null values. Limited-horizon experiments report state-of-the-art results, supporting the value of adapting betting behavior to both accumulated evidence and remaining time.
icml-2026-learning-to-bet-for-horizon-aw.tldr: A learned betting policy adapts anytime-valid tests to deadlines using theoretical guidance on when to bet more or less aggressively.

paragraphs: When feedback arrives only at the end of a sampled rollout and indicates success or failure, a model induces a likelihood over successful rollouts. This paper argues that this likelihood provides a natural training objective. Reinforcement learning is commonly used in this setting because the feedback cannot be differentiated directly through the sampled outcome.

The authors prove that standard expected-reward reinforcement learning gives only a first-order approximation to the likelihood objective. They introduce Maximum Likelihood Reinforcement Learning, or MaxRL, as a family of sample-based objectives indexed by available computation. Increasing sampling compute moves the objective from expected-reward learning toward maximum likelihood, making the training criterion itself responsive to the sampling budget.

The proposed objective requires a one-line change to standard reinforcement-learning implementations. Across all tested models and tasks, the authors report Pareto dominance over existing methods, up to twentyfold gains in test-time scaling efficiency over GRPO, and more favorable scaling with training data and compute. These empirical findings concern the evaluated settings with terminal binary feedback.
icml-2026-maximum-likelihood-reinforceme.tldr: MaxRL uses increasing sampling compute to move from expected-reward training toward maximum likelihood for tasks with terminal binary feedback.

paragraphs: Tsetlin Machines classify using propositional clauses, but obtaining a small accurate collection is difficult. Training with few clauses can struggle to find the necessary precise rules. Pruning a larger trained model also presents a problem: clauses interact logically, so a clause that appears dispensable alone may become essential after other clauses are removed.

The authors formalize compression as finding the smallest clause subset that preserves the trained model’s discrimination of training samples. They prove this Minimum Discriminating Clause Set problem is NP-hard and formulate its solution using weighted partial Maximum Satisfiability. A partition-and-merge strategy extends the approach to datasets containing 100,000 samples.

Across thirteen datasets, compressed models use a median of sixteen clauses while remaining within a few percentage points of a 200-clause teacher’s accuracy. They outperform directly trained models of matching capacity on every dataset where direct training has room to improve, with gains reaching 45 percentage points. These results support selecting logically compatible subsets from larger models as an effective route to compact classifiers.
icml-2026-maxsat-based-compression-for-t.tldr: MaxSAT-based clause selection compresses trained Tsetlin Machines substantially while retaining accuracy close to their larger teachers.

paragraphs: The paper studies Gaussian process Thompson sampling, a widely used Bayesian optimization method, assuming the objective function is a sample path from a Gaussian process. It examines regret: the performance lost through choices that fall short of the optimum. Earlier analyses of this method mostly addressed expected regret, leaving questions about guarantees beyond the average.

A central result is a regret lower bound showing that, with probability δ, the method suffers regret with polynomial dependence on 1/δ. This establishes a constraint on how favorable guarantees can become as the permitted failure probability decreases. The authors also bound the second moment of cumulative regret, which accounts for squared regret and directly suggests an improved upper bound in terms of δ.

The paper additionally establishes expected lenient regret upper bounds and improves a cumulative regret upper bound in its dependence on the number of optimization steps, T. These results address whether types of guarantees recently developed for Gaussian process upper confidence bound methods can also be established for Thompson sampling.

Supporting lemmas relax a condition used in recent analysis to obtain improved bounds in T. Together, the findings sharpen the theoretical picture of Thompson sampling under the stated Gaussian process assumption, covering both achievable guarantees and constraints on those guarantees.
icml-2026-on-regret-bounds-of-thompson-s.tldr: Under a Gaussian process assumption, the paper establishes new regret bounds for Thompson sampling, improving guarantees while identifying limits on their dependence on failure probability.

paragraphs: Network embeddings represent nodes as points in a geometric space, with the goal of recovering underlying latent positions. Existing consistency guarantees often assume that the embedding dimension is correct. This paper studies what happens when that choice is wrong under the random dot product graph model, a family that includes stochastic blockmodels.

The analysis reveals an asymmetry between choosing too many dimensions and choosing too few. With an oversized embedding, latent-position estimates remain consistent under the studied assumptions, although convergence is slower than with the correct dimension. With an undersized embedding, a fundamental error lower bound need not disappear even as the network grows arbitrarily large.

Synthetic experiments support these theoretical predictions. The technical analysis also generalizes a random-matrix result showing that all non-signal eigenvectors of a low-rank matrix with additive noise are delocalized. The practical meaning of the main result is that dimension errors have qualitatively different consequences: extra dimensions can slow recovery, while omitted dimensions can leave persistent estimation error in the analyzed model class.
icml-2026-on-the-effect-of-misspecifying.tldr: For random dot product graphs, oversized embeddings remain consistent more slowly, while undersized embeddings can retain irreducible estimation error.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires adapting to new tasks while retaining performance on earlier ones. This paper analyzes forgetting in a deliberately tractable neural-network setting: a single hidden layer with quadratic units, trained by gradient descent on successive noisy XOR-cluster datasets. Different tasks have orthogonal cluster means, providing a structured basis for studying their interactions.

The authors tightly characterize how training loss evolves under gradient descent. From these dynamics, they derive explicit bounds on forgetting during training as functions of iteration count, sample size, number of tasks, and hidden-layer width. This makes several influences on forgetting visible within one mathematical account.

They then use algorithmic stability to bound the gap between training and generalization behavior, obtaining corresponding guarantees for forgetting on test data. Numerical experiments corroborate the analysis. The work provides closed-form forgetting guarantees within its specified network and data setting, explaining how optimization progress and problem size jointly shape retention rather than treating forgetting as an unexplained consequence of sequential training.
icml-2026-on-the-theory-of-continual-lea.tldr: The paper derives explicit training- and test-time forgetting bounds for quadratic neural networks learning a structured sequence of noisy tasks.

paragraphs: Robustness guarantees must account for the randomness of training if they are to describe the models that training actually produces. This paper treats gradient-based training as a discrete-time stochastic dynamical system. Adversarial robustness then becomes a safety-verification problem concerning whether the final parameters remain within a designated safe set.

The authors use barrier certificates to derive sufficient conditions for probabilistic robustness against worst-case perturbations bounded in an l-p norm. They represent these certificates with neural networks and obtain probably approximately correct guarantees through a scenario convex problem. This makes both training randomness and the confidence attached to certification explicit parts of the framework.

The method identifies the largest certified radius for which its probabilistic accuracy requirement holds at a specified confidence level. Experiments on MNIST, SVHN, and CIFAR-10 demonstrate formal guarantees under stochastic training without requiring a particular model family or advance knowledge of the attack strategy. The guarantee remains probabilistic and applies within the certified perturbation radius; the sufficient certification conditions do not establish unrestricted immunity to attacks.
icml-2026-probabilistic-robustness-certi.tldr: Barrier certificates provide probabilistic adversarial-robustness guarantees that explicitly account for stochastic training and bounded worst-case perturbations.

paragraphs: Appending filler symbols gives a transformer additional positions in which to perform computation. This paper uses polynomial amounts of such padding to characterize transformer expressivity through Boolean circuit classes. It asks which architectural choices change computational power and which leave these equivalences intact under the assumptions studied.

The authors prove that L-uniform constant-precision padded transformers correspond exactly to L-uniform AC0, while growing precision yields L-uniform TC0 regardless of width. These circuit-class characterizations separate the role of numerical precision from the size of the model’s representations. Both softmax attention and average hard attention satisfy the reported results.

Looping adds another dimension of computational power. With log-to-the-d N loops, constant-precision models reach FO-uniform ACd, while growing-precision models reach FO-uniform TCd. Increasing width or precision beyond logarithmic scale does not further increase expressivity in these characterizations. The findings identify precision and computational depth as the main factors, while showing robustness to several other modeling choices that had complicated earlier comparisons.
icml-2026-revisiting-padded-transformer-.tldr: Circuit-class equivalences show that precision and depth chiefly determine padded-transformer expressivity under the studied assumptions.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to estimate the mean of private, multidimensional data when each user sends one randomized message. The analyzer receives only the shuffled collection of reports. A mechanism designed to be optimal under local differential privacy may not make the best use of the privacy properties available after shuffling.

The authors formulate mechanism design after shuffling as an explicit optimization problem using a quantity called the shuffle index. They derive a lower bound on achievable mean squared error in terms of this index. The bound shows that local-privacy optimality does not necessarily survive the addition of shuffling, motivating mechanisms designed for the complete reporting process.

They then construct an asymptotically optimal unbiased estimator in the high-privacy regime. Its privacy–utility trade-off is nearly the same as that of the central Gaussian mechanism. This result connects a restricted communication setting—one message per user—with accuracy approaching that central reference, while retaining the stated high-privacy and asymptotic qualifications.
icml-2026-shuffling-aware-optimization-f.tldr: Optimizing private mean estimation specifically for shuffling yields an asymptotically optimal high-privacy mechanism with nearly central-Gaussian utility.

paragraphs: Producing several sizes of a reasoning model usually requires separate training or compression runs. Star Elastic instead adds nested submodels to a parent model in one post-training job. These submodels also allow computation to change between the thinking and answering phases, creating a way to adjust the reasoning budget during use.

The method supports nesting across state-space, embedding-channel, mixture-of-experts, and feed-forward components. It combines an end-to-end trainable router with curriculum-based knowledge distillation. Applied to Nemotron Nano v3, it produces 23-billion- and 12-billion-parameter variants from a 30-billion-parameter parent; applications to Nano v2 produce 9-billion- and 6-billion-parameter nested models.

The authors report that all evaluated nested models match or exceed independently trained baselines of similar size. For Nano v2, they report reductions of 360-fold relative to training from scratch and sevenfold relative to state-of-the-art compression methods. Dynamic selection between reasoning phases improves the reported accuracy–latency frontier, with gains reaching 16% higher accuracy and 1.9-fold lower latency. These are reported maxima, not uniform improvements for every budget.
icml-2026-star-elastic-many-in-one-reaso.tldr: Star Elastic creates nested reasoning models in one post-training run and adjusts model size between thinking and answering to improve accuracy–latency trade-offs.

paragraphs: The HiPPO matrix has been used within an LSSL, a lightweight model for processing sequences. This paper introduces a mathematical object called the Continuized-HiPPO Operator by taking a continuous limit of that matrix. The contribution focuses on what this operator formulation makes possible to analyze about the associated state-space model.

One result concerns the asymptotic behavior of eigenvalues of a matrix related to HiPPO. Instead of treating the matrix only as a finite computational object, the continuous-limit construction provides a route to studying its spectral behavior. This is one of the concrete analytical advantages the authors establish for the proposed operator.

The other result is an explicit solution for the LSSL induced by the continuous-limit operator. The two contributions address complementary questions: how a related matrix’s eigenvalues behave asymptotically, and how the limiting sequence model can be solved explicitly. The paper thus supplies an analytical formulation of HiPPO-based sequence processing whose stated benefits are spectral analysis and a solution formula.
icml-2026-state-space-model-with-continu.tldr: A continuous-limit HiPPO operator enables asymptotic eigenvalue analysis and an explicit solution for its induced sequence-processing model.

paragraphs: Training on the same sources in different orders can produce different outcomes, and the number of possible curricula grows factorially. This paper characterizes the local effect of swapping two sources through the Lie bracket of their gradient-update fields. That quantity yields a score predicting which order is better for a target domain.

The pairwise score also supports a tournament over many sources. With a shared initial target-gradient reference, Hessian symmetry allows row-sum rankings using one Hessian-vector product per source, a linear number of dot products, and a sort. The planner therefore avoids explicitly building the quadratic matrix of every pairwise comparison.

Empirically, pairwise accuracy is about 98% for instruction tuning and preference optimization at k=1, falling to about 72–73% at k=20. At curriculum scale, the method finds the best of six schedules in 87.5% of trials and achieves high sampled-percentile rankings on larger domain collections. These results support local update geometry as a useful scheduling signal, while the declining accuracy shows that predictive strength varies across the evaluated settings.
icml-2026-the-geometry-of-sequential-lea.tldr: Lie brackets predict local training-order effects and enable scalable curriculum rankings without evaluating every source pair.

paragraphs: Models can use the same vocabulary and exhibit identical internal representations while requiring very different learning updates. This paper studies that problem for training-free source selection, including scientific sequence domains. In a shared-output-head setting, the authors show that representation similarity alone cannot identify transfer relationships: identical representations can coexist with orthogonal head updates.

Their key identity expresses head Fisher alignment as a cosine between kernel mean embeddings in a joint space of activations and errors. This separates contributions from activations, errors, and their coupling without constructing a full Fisher matrix. FisherSketch estimates the cosine in one streaming pass, producing a 16 KB task signature with a 192 KB streaming state per task.

The signatures also serve as diagnostic tools for understanding what makes tasks similar. Validations involving shared parameters, internal layers, and verbalizer shifts show that FisherSketch remains informative when activation similarity cannot distinguish tasks. The contribution makes transfer-relevant update structure practical to summarize at vocabulary scale while explaining why matching representations can overlook differences in learning targets.
icml-2026-the-geometry-of-updates-fisher.tldr: FisherSketch compactly estimates update alignment from activations and errors, distinguishing tasks that representation similarity alone cannot separate.

paragraphs: Steering a language model changes its intermediate representations along a chosen direction during inference. Selecting the direction receives considerable attention, but the size of the intervention is equally consequential. A small change may fail to induce the intended behavior, while an excessive change can severely damage performance.

This paper develops a theoretical analysis of steering strength. It characterizes how intervention magnitude affects next-token probability, the presence of a concept, and cross-entropy. Examining these quantities together connects the immediate output distribution with the intended behavioral effect and with a measure of predictive performance.

The analysis produces qualitative laws, including non-monotonic behavior: increasing steering strength need not continue changing an outcome in the same direction. The authors empirically validate their predictions on eleven language models spanning a small GPT architecture and modern models. The findings establish that strength is a substantive part of the intervention, whose effects cannot generally be understood by assuming that more movement along a chosen direction always produces more of the desired behavior.
icml-2026-towards-understanding-steering.tldr: Theory and experiments show that steering strength can affect language-model behavior non-monotonically, making intervention magnitude crucial to effective control.

paragraphs: A retrieval system can miss an entity that is relevant to a question because its embedding has low similarity to the query embedding. This paper calls such failures blind spots and investigates how training biases place relevant entities in poorly retrievable regions of the embedding space. These omissions can deprive retrieval-augmented generation of needed information.

The authors introduce a Retrieval Probability Score that predicts blind-spot risk from entity embedding geometry before indexing. Using data built from Wikidata relations and Wikipedia introductions, they show that this assessment can avoid expensive retrieval evaluations. Their ARGUS pipeline then targets low-scoring entities with document augmentation drawn from a knowledge base.

Experiments on BRIGHT, ImpliRet, and RAR-b show consistent improvements across all evaluated retrievers. Average gains are 3.4 absolute nDCG@5 points and 4.5 nDCG@10 points, with larger gains on challenging subsets. The results support diagnosing and addressing likely retrieval failures before they appear in downstream answers, using targeted augmentation to improve access to information already relevant to the query.
icml-2026-with-argus-eyes-assessing-retr.tldr: ARGUS predicts retrieval blind spots from embedding geometry and improves retrieval through targeted augmentation of high-risk entities.
